findings.finding: The plan uses a classic `repo`-scope personal access token for the cross-repo dispatch without considering the established, narrower credentials. A classic `repo` token grants full read/write to every private and public repo its owner can reach, not just the tap. GitHub's documented pattern for triggering a workflow from another workflow is a GitHub App installation token (actions/create-github-app-token, short-lived, scoped to the installed repos and the Actions permission) or a fine-grained PAT. A fine-grained PAT can be limited to navapbc/homebrew-rebar with Actions read/write, which is enough for `gh api .../workflows/autobump.yml`, `gh workflow enable` and `gh workflow run`. The plan also reverses the repo's documented no-stored-token posture without explaining why these alternatives were rejected.

scenarios: The secret leaks (for example through a compromised dependency in a future step of the job, or a mis-scoped log). The attacker then gets write access to every repo the owner can reach, not just permission to dispatch one tap workflow.
The classic PAT is tied to one person's account. If that person leaves navapbc or the token expires, the release job's tap dispatch fails, with no rotation path documented beyond the SSM copy.

findings.finding: The plan says the new run step 'carries a `# mechanism-ok: ci_gate` marker naming this ticket'. The marker grammar in markers.py does not work that way. A marker must be `# mechanism-ok: <kind> <name> — <reason or ticket id>`, and it admits only its exact `kind::name` key. For a workflow step, the name is `.github/workflows/release.yml::<step name>` (or the first 60 characters of the run text if the step has no name), and the marker must sit on the step's name/run line or the line just above it. The plan gives no step name and no site key. A marker with only `ci_gate` plus a ticket id would parse the ticket id as the name, admit nothing, and the mechanism-delta ratchet would still flag the new step.
findings.location: Approach — final paragraph ('carries a `# mechanism-ok: ci_gate` marker naming this ticket'); .github/workflows/release.yml new homebrew_tap step

findings.finding: The plan stores HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN as a repository-level Actions secret. Every workflow in navapbc/rebar, on any branch, can read it. The repo's only other privileged release step (publish) runs in the `pypi` environment, which requires reviewers and a main-only policy, and the authorize job checks that policy. The homebrew_tap job declares no environment, so the cross-repo token is not covered by those protections.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Change the wait to pass once PyPI's `info.version` is >= inputs.version (PEP 440 comparison), not only on exact equality, so a newer latest does not fail the job.
evidence: Plan: 'until `https://pypi.org/pypi/nava-rebar/json` reports `info.version == inputs.version`'.

mcp_registry's wait (release.yml:400-415) polls the version-specific endpoint `/pypi/nava-rebar/${version}/json` for 200. A newer release does not break that check, but the plan's equality on the unversioned `info.version` breaks in this case.
findings.finding: The PyPI wait requires `info.version == inputs.version` exactly. When a newer version is already PyPI's latest, the check can never pass: either the release workflow is re-run, or two releases go out close together and the older run's homebrew_tap job runs after the newer version is live. The job then sleeps 5 minutes and fails the release run, even though the tap would correctly bump to the newer latest.
scenarios: A maintainer re-runs the failed jobs of release 0.16.0 after 0.16.1 has shipped. homebrew_tap waits 5 minutes and fails.
Two releases go out minutes apart. The first run's homebrew_tap sees `info.version` already at the second version and fails.
findings.suggested_fix: Inside the loop: `latest=$(curl -fsS https://pypi.org/pypi/nava-rebar/json | python3 -c 'import json,sys;print(json.load(sys.stdin)["info"]["version"])')`, then exit 0 if `python3 -c 'import sys;from itertools import zip_longest as z;a,b=([int(x) for x in v.split(".")] for v in sys.argv[1:]);sys.exit(0 if [p or 0 for p,_ in z(a,b)]>=[q or 0 for _,q in z(a,b)] else 1)' "$latest" "$VERSION"` succeeds. This uses only the stdlib, since the job has no checkout or extra installs; it is valid because releases are plain X.Y.Z with no rc forms.

findings.finding: The PyPI wait uses a different surface from the mcp_registry step it claims to copy. It polls the project-level `info.version` (PyPI's latest) instead of the per-version endpoint's HTTP 200. Whenever the dispatched version is not PyPI's latest (a backport or patch to an older line, or a prerelease that PyPI doesn't report as latest), the loop can never match and the job fails after 5 minutes. Also, the wait runs on rebar's runner, while the tap's script queries PyPI later from its own runner, so CDN freshness is not guaranteed there.
scenarios: Releasing 0.13.2 after 0.16.0 is latest: the wait times out and the release run shows a red job
The tap's runner gets a stale CDN answer and its run no-ops successfully
